name: Dejerine-Sottas disease
aliases: hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type III

reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A severe, early-onset hereditary demyelinating neuropathy historically classified as hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type III, at the severe end of the Charcot-Marie-Tooth spectrum
Presents in infancy or early childhood with marked hypotonia, delayed motor milestones, and progressive distal then generalised weakness
Nerve conduction velocities are profoundly slowed, reflecting severe demyelination, and cerebrospinal fluid protein may be elevated
Peripheral nerves may be palpably enlarged due to hypertrophic onion-bulb formation from repeated demyelination and remyelination
It is caused by mutations in the same myelin-related genes implicated in other CMT forms, such as PMP22, MPZ, and EGR2, often as severe de novo or biallelic mutations
Sensory loss, areflexia, skeletal deformity, and sometimes ataxia accompany the weakness
Diagnosis combines the early severe phenotype, very slow conduction, and genetic testing across the relevant myelin genes
Care is supportive with rehabilitation, orthotics, and management of deformity, as there is no specific cure
reference.pathophysiology: Dejerine-Sottas disease is a hypertrophic demyelinating neuropathy caused by mutations affecting proteins critical for peripheral myelin formation and maintenance. Severe or biallelic mutations in genes such as PMP22, MPZ, and EGR2 produce profound failure of Schwann cell myelination beginning early in life, with repeated cycles of demyelination and attempted remyelination generating the onion-bulb hypertrophy that can enlarge nerves. The severe, diffuse demyelination markedly slows conduction and causes early, disabling motor and sensory deficits.
additionalDifferentials: Other Charcot-Marie-Tooth subtypes, including congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy of childhood
Spinal muscular atrophy and congenital myopathies
Other causes of the floppy infant
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies showing markedly slowed velocities
Genetic testing across PMP22, MPZ, EGR2 and related myelin genes
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis when the presentation overlaps with inflammatory neuropathy
Nerve imaging or examination for hypertrophy
redFlags: Marked hypotonia and respiratory difficulty in infancy
Rapid loss of motor function or bulbar involvement
Features suggesting a treatable inflammatory neuropathy
Severe skeletal deformity compromising function or respiration
reference.prognosis: The disorder is generally more severe and disabling than typical Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, often with early and significant motor impairment, though the course varies with the underlying mutation; management remains supportive.
pitfalls: Overlooking a steroid-responsive inflammatory neuropathy that can mimic the severe demyelinating picture
Assuming a single gene and not testing the range of relevant myelin genes
Underestimating the value of early rehabilitation and orthopaedic care
Failing to provide genetic counselling given de novo and recessive inheritance patterns
management: Supportive management as no disease-modifying therapy exists, anchored in physiotherapy to preserve strength, maintain range of movement and delay contractures
Occupational therapy, ankle-foot orthoses and mobility aids to support delayed motor milestones and progressive distal weakness
Orthopaedic assessment and management of skeletal deformity and joint contractures, including surgery where indicated
Neuropathic pain control with appropriate neuropathic agents
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine that aggravate the demyelinating neuropathy
Early developmental and rehabilitation input given infantile onset and disability
Genetic counselling with confirmatory testing of PMP22, MPZ and EGR2 and family screening, noting many cases are severe de novo or biallelic mutations
